# Frameworks and Automatic Differentiation {#sec-frameworks-autodiff}

A machine-learning framework defines the executable contract between model code
and hardware. That contract covers tensor values, operator semantics, derivative
rules, device placement, distributed layout, and execution mode. A program can
be mathematically sound and still fail because one of these parts is undefined,
unsupported, or interpreted differently by another backend.

This chapter follows that contract from a scalar loss to the work performed on
devices. It first explains automatic differentiation, then the memory and
correctness obligations of reverse mode, and finally the framework machinery
that captures, compiles, dispatches, and distributes the resulting program. The
hardware limits underneath it are introduced in @sec-accelerators-networking;
the compiler and kernel pipeline continues in @sec-compilers-kernels.

## Three ways to obtain a derivative

Finite differences estimate a derivative by perturbing an input. For a scalar
function $f$ evaluated at $x$, the forward-difference estimate for coordinate
$i$ is

$$
g_i^{(h)}=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x)}{h}
=\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x_i}
+O(h)+O\!\left(\frac{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}}{h}\right).
$$

Here, $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the input, $e_i$ is the basis vector whose $i$th
entry is one, $h$ is the nonzero step size, and $g_i^{(h)}$ is the estimate.
The $O(h)$ term represents truncation error, while the
$O(\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}/h)$ term represents scale-dependent floating-point
round-off and cancellation. A smaller step reduces one error and can amplify
the other. Computing every coordinate also requires one perturbation per input
for forward differences, or two for central differences. That is unsuitable
for producing a billion-parameter training gradient, although directional
finite differences remain valuable as a gradient check.
@fig-frameworks-autodiff-step measures both errors for one function.

```{figure}
//| figure: finite-difference-step
//| label: fig-frameworks-autodiff-step
//| fig-cap: "Error of the forward and central differences against the step $h$ for the runnable's $f(t)=t^2+\sin t$ at $x=2$, computed in the page in float64 or float32 arithmetic and compared with the exact $f'(x)=2x+\cos x$. As $h$ grows from a tiny step, round-off $O(\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}/h)$ falls until truncation takes over, $O(h)$ for the forward difference and $O(h^2)$ for the central one, so each method has a best step and a smaller $h$ only adds error. The dashed guides are those leading terms with this function's constants. In float32 the smallest errors are several orders of magnitude larger, which is why a gradient check runs in double precision."
```

Symbolic differentiation transforms a mathematical expression into another
expression. It can produce a useful closed form, but naive expansion can repeat
shared subexpressions and cause expression swell. Control flow, mutation, calls
into external libraries, and large tensor programs also require a richer
program representation than an ordinary computer-algebra expression.

The third method, @gls-autodiff, composes a local derivative rule for each
primitive in an executed numerical program while preserving the program's
intermediate structure [@baydin2018survey]. The implementation may record an
eager tape (a log of the operations in the order they ran), trace a graph,
transform an intermediate representation, or rewrite source code. In ideal
arithmetic it applies the chain rule exactly to the selected differentiable
path; on a machine it evaluates that derivative at machine precision and still
incurs rounding, overflow, and underflow. It does not differentiate a discrete
branch decision. At a nondifferentiable point, the framework must choose a
convention, return an undefined value, or raise an error.

The history predates neural-network libraries. Wengert described a linear list
of elementary evaluations in 1964 [@wengert1964]. Linnainmaa developed reverse
accumulation for computer programs, and the method was later popularized for
neural networks as backpropagation [@linnainmaa1976; @rumelhart1986]. Modern
frameworks generalize that idea from scalar arithmetic to tensor operators.

## Linearization is the core interface

Consider a differentiable function

$$
f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m.
$$

Here, $n$ is the input dimension, $m$ is the output dimension, and
$x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is the point at which the function is evaluated. The
Jacobian $J_f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ contains every local sensitivity,
with entry $(j,i)$ equal to $\partial f_j(x)/\partial x_i$. Frameworks rarely
need to materialize that whole matrix; they need its action on a vector.

Forward mode computes a Jacobian-vector product (JVP),

$$
\operatorname{JVP}_f(x;v)=J_f(x)v\in\mathbb{R}^m,
$$

where $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is an input tangent, a direction of change in the
input. A basis tangent $v=e_i$ returns one column of the Jacobian, while an
arbitrary $v$ returns a directional derivative. Forward mode propagates the
tangent alongside each intermediate and does not need to retain a reverse tape.

Reverse mode computes a vector-Jacobian product (VJP),

$$
\operatorname{VJP}_f(x;u)=J_f(x)^\mathsf{T}u\in\mathbb{R}^n,
$$

where $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$ is an output cotangent, a weighting over the outputs,
and $\mathsf{T}$ denotes transpose. A basis cotangent returns one Jacobian row,
transposed. If $L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is a scalar loss, the single
number that training minimizes, then $m=1$ and the output seed $u=1$ produces
the entire gradient in one reverse sweep:

$$
\nabla L(x)=J_L(x)^\mathsf{T}1.
$$

The shape of the Jacobian determines the mode choice. A full Jacobian can be
assembled from $n$ JVP columns or $m$ VJP rows, unless batching or structure
reduces the work. Neural-network training has many inputs and one scalar loss,
so reverse mode is the natural fit. Forward mode remains useful for directional
derivatives, functions with few inputs and many outputs, and compositions such
as Hessian-vector products [@jax2026autodiff].

The cheap-gradient result is a statement about operation counts, not about
wall-clock time. Baur and Strassen proved a constant-factor bound for a
rational straight-line computation, meaning a branch-free sequence of
arithmetic operations, together with all of its first partial derivatives
under a particular operation-count convention [@baur1983]. More generally, when
primitive VJP rules have bounded relative cost, reverse arithmetic is
$O(C_f)$ for a scalar function whose evaluation costs $C_f$. The bound does not
include saved-tensor traffic, kernel launches, communication, synchronization,
or the storage and writing of $n$ gradient values. Real backward time need not
be a fixed multiple of forward time.

## How reverse accumulation works

An eager engine, which runs each operation as soon as the program calls it,
records a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the tensor operations that ran. Each
node holds an output value and a backward rule that maps an incoming output
adjoint, the sensitivity of the loss to that node's output, to contributions
for its parents. In scalar notation, if node $v_i$ is consumed by later nodes,
its accumulated adjoint is

$$
\bar v_i=\sum_{j\in\operatorname{succ}(i)}
\bar v_j\frac{\partial v_j}{\partial v_i}.
$$

Here, $\bar v_i=\partial L/\partial v_i$ is the loss sensitivity of node
$v_i$, $\operatorname{succ}(i)$ denotes its direct successors, and the sum
collects one contribution from every use. Each node accumulates those
contributions. The adjoint of the scalar output is seeded with one. Nodes are
then processed in reverse topological order, so all downstream contributions
have arrived before a node sends gradients to its parents. Vector-valued
operators apply the transpose of a local Jacobian rather than a scalar
derivative.

```text
forward:
  execute each primitive and record its parents plus its local VJP rule

reverse:
  set every adjoint to zero and set the scalar output adjoint to one
  visit nodes once in reverse topological order
  add each node's VJP contribution to every parent adjoint
```

For $v_1=xy$, $v_2=\sin(x)$, and $z=v_1+v_2$, the backward sweep gives
$\bar z=1$, $\bar v_1=\bar v_2=1$,
$\bar x=\bar v_1y+\bar v_2\cos(x)=y+\cos(x)$, and
$\bar y=\bar v_1x=x$. The two contributions to $x$ must be added.

```{figure}
//| figure: reverse-accumulation
//| label: fig-frameworks-autodiff-tape
//| fig-cap: "Reverse accumulation on a recorded graph, computed in the page for the chosen $x$ and $y$. The forward pass fills in each node's value; the reverse sweep seeds $\bar z=1$ and sends one contribution $\bar v_j\,\partial v_j/\partial v_i$ along each edge, whose label is the local derivative. In $z=xy+\sin(x)$, $x$ has two consumers and receives two terms, $\bar x=y+\cos(x)$. The second graph is the runnable's $z=a+a$ with $a=x^2$: reverse topological order gives $\bar x=4x$, while the recursive schedule that propagates an already accumulated adjoint once per path counts a path twice and returns $6x$. The last step checks the sweep against a centered finite difference."
```

The following runnable implements the scheduling invariant directly. The first
case deliberately reuses a non-leaf node: $a=x^2$ and $z=a+a$. A recursive
backward routine that propagates an already accumulated adjoint once per path
returns the wrong answer for this graph. Topological scheduling processes each
node once and returns $\mathrm{d}z/\mathrm{d}x=4x=8$ at $x=2$.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
import math

class Var:
    def __init__(self, val, parents=()):
        self.val = float(val)
        self.parents = tuple(parents)  # (parent, local derivative)
        self.grad = 0.0

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Var(self.val + other.val, ((self, 1.0), (other, 1.0)))

    def __mul__(self, other):
        return Var(self.val * other.val, ((self, other.val), (other, self.val)))

    def backward(self, seed=1.0):
        order = topo(self)
        for node in order:
            node.grad = 0.0
        self.grad = seed
        for node in reversed(order):
            for parent, local in node.parents:
                parent.grad += node.grad * local

def sin(value):
    return Var(math.sin(value.val), ((value, math.cos(value.val)),))

def topo(root):
    order, seen = [], set()
    def visit(node):
        if node in seen:
            return
        seen.add(node)
        for parent, _ in node.parents:
            visit(parent)
        order.append(node)
    visit(root)
    return order

def finite_difference(fn, x, h=1e-6):
    return (fn(x + h) - fn(x - h)) / (2 * h)

x = Var(2.0)
a = x * x
z = a + a
z.backward()
print("shared analytic", x.grad, "expected", 8.0)

x = Var(2.0)
z = x * x + sin(x)
z.backward()
numeric = finite_difference(lambda t: t * t + math.sin(t), 2.0)
print("finite difference", round(numeric, 6), "analytic", round(x.grad, 6))
```
::::

Real engines store vector VJP functions and only the saved tensors needed by
those functions; they do not store a scalar local derivative on every edge.
They also distinguish two kinds of accumulation. Fan-out contributions are
summed inside one backward graph. Separately, parameter `.grad` buffers often
persist across backward calls, so an optimizer loop, the code that updates
parameters from their gradients, clears the buffers between steps
[@pytorch2026autograd].

## Differentiability is part of the operator contract

Automatic differentiation is only as correct as the primitive rules it
composes. Several cases require an explicit decision:

- A nondifferentiable operation may use a documented subgradient, return zero,
  propagate a `NaN`, or reject the request. Ties in `max`, clipping boundaries,
  indices, sorting, and integer outputs deserve tests rather than assumptions.
- A detach or stop-gradient operation intentionally cuts a path. Accidentally
  copying a tensor through an API that drops history can do the same thing.
- In-place mutation or an incorrect alias declaration can overwrite a value
  saved for backward. Framework version counters catch many cases, but a custom
  operator still has to declare mutation and aliasing correctly.
- A custom derivative can connect external code to autodiff, but its backward,
  JVP, batching, autocast (automatic casting to lower precision), tracing, and
  higher-order behavior are separate
  contracts. If an operation can be expressed with built-in tensor operators,
  composition usually preserves more of those contracts automatically
  [@pytorch2026extending].
- Mixed precision, which runs selected operations in a lower-precision format,
  changes both value and gradient numerics. FP16 training may need loss
  scaling, which multiplies the loss by a constant so that small gradients do
  not underflow; gradients must be unscaled before clipping or inspection, and
  `NaN` or infinity detection belongs in the optimizer protocol.

A gradient check compares an analytical directional derivative with a centered
finite difference in double precision, away from discontinuities. For a
high-dimensional input, the check picks a direction $r$ and compares
$\nabla L(x)^\mathsf{T}r$ with
$[L(x+hr)-L(x-hr)]/(2h)$. Here, $r$ is the test direction and $h$ is the finite
difference step. This checks the whole gradient along one direction without
constructing a coordinate-wise numerical gradient. Custom rules should also be
checked at zero-size, broadcast, noncontiguous, and extreme inputs, and should
receive a second-order gradient check if higher derivatives are promised
[@pytorch2026gradcheck].

## Reverse-mode memory and recomputation

The forward pass saves tensors required by later VJP rules. It does not
necessarily retain every intermediate, and saved tensors can be released as
backward consumes them. Even so, these saved intermediates, called activations,
can occupy far more memory than the dynamic graph's metadata. Total training
memory also includes parameters, gradients, optimizer
state, temporary workspaces, communication buffers, and allocator reserves.

Activation checkpointing omits selected saved tensors and reruns part of the
forward computation during backward. For a uniform chain of $n$ stages divided
into segments of $k$ stages, a simple model for the number of simultaneously
stored activation states is

$$
M(k)\approx\left\lceil\frac{n}{k}\right\rceil+k.
$$

Here, $M(k)$ is the peak saved-state count, $n$ is the chain length, $k$ is the
segment length, and $\lceil\cdot\rceil$ rounds upward. Choosing
$k\approx\sqrt{n}$ gives $M(k)=O(\!\sqrt{n})$ while recomputing each segment at
most once [@chen2016sublinear]. Recursive schedules can reach different
time-memory points. These bounds do not transfer unchanged to arbitrary DAGs,
unequal activation sizes, skip connections, or communication-heavy graphs.

Recomputation must reproduce the original forward values. A changed
random-number-generator state, mutable global, device move, or other side
effect can make the recomputed path differ and can yield a silent gradient
error. Framework checkpoint utilities preserve some random-number-generator
state, but the exact device and state coverage is part of their documented
contract [@pytorch2026checkpoint]. Checkpointing may lower peak memory while
increasing arithmetic, communication exposure, or step time, so its net effect
has to be measured on the real workload.

## Eager, traced, and compiled are different axes

Early tensor systems exposed the representation they needed for optimization.
Theano constructed symbolic graphs, and TensorFlow 1 executed a static dataflow
graph through a session [@theano2016framework; @abadi2016tensorflow]. Chainer and
PyTorch made eager execution practical by recording the operations of each
concrete run; PyTorch's design kept ordinary Python control flow while moving
its tensor hot path below Python [@paszke2019pytorch]. JAX took another route:
transform pure functions through tracing, and compose differentiation,
vectorization, and compilation as program transformations [@frostig2018jax].

Current systems combine these approaches, pairing immediate execution with one
or more staged representations:

| Mode | What happens | What can be reused | Main failure modes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eager execution | Operators run as host code dispatches them; an autodiff DAG may still be recorded. | Kernel and allocator caches | Host overhead, less fusion, accidental mutation |
| Tracing or staging | A function runs with abstract or symbolic values to produce an intermediate graph. | A graph specialized to an input signature | Trace-time side effects, unsupported data-dependent control flow, retracing |
| Guarded graph capture | Regions of a dynamic host program are captured while assumptions are recorded. | A cached executable while its guards hold | Graph break, guard failure, recompilation, compile latency |
| Ahead-of-time export | A bounded program and input contract are lowered before deployment. | A serialized artifact for that contract | Unsupported dynamic behavior, mismatched runtime assumptions |

In PyTorch eager mode, autograd rebuilds a `Function` DAG on every recorded
forward pass. `torch.compile` is a separate capture path: TorchDynamo extracts
FX regions, records guards over assumptions such as type, shape, dtype, device,
and stride, then sends captured graphs through AOTAutograd and a backend. With
partial capture, unsupported code creates a graph break and execution can resume
in another captured region. A failed guard can select another cached executable
or trigger recompilation; requiring a full graph turns a break into an error
[@ansel2024pytorch2; @pytorch2026compile].

JAX's `grad` and `vmap` are transformations, while `jit` stages and compiles a
specialization. Compatible calls reuse the cached executable. Ordinary Python
side effects occur during tracing rather than on every device execution, and a
runtime data-dependent branch inside a jitted region needs a structured control
flow primitive or a different staging boundary [@jax2026jit]. TensorFlow 2
executes eagerly by default; `GradientTape` records eager TensorFlow operations,
while `tf.function` traces and caches specialized TensorFlow graphs. XLA
compilation is an additional choice, not a synonym for `tf.function`
[@tensorflow2026autodiff; @tensorflow2026function].

A useful comparison of these modes therefore asks which semantics are visible
at trace time, what becomes part of the cache key, which effects remain
observable, how failures fall back, and whether cold compile cost is amortized
by warm execution.

## What a framework must specify

A modern framework specifies a set of cross-cutting contracts, and a single
tensor operation has to satisfy several of them at once:

1. A tensor representation defines shape, dtype, device, layout, strides,
   aliases, gradient state, and sometimes distributed placement.
2. An operator schema defines accepted inputs, broadcasting, dtype promotion,
   output metadata, mutation, and aliasing.
3. A dispatcher selects implementations by backend and also by transformation
   or mode, such as autograd, batching, autocast, functionalization (rewriting
   mutation as pure operations), and tensor subclasses.
4. An autodiff transform supplies VJP and, when supported, JVP rules plus the
   saved-tensor contract.
5. A compiler needs abstract or fake-tensor behavior, in which tensors carry
   shape and dtype metadata but no data, as well as graph lowering, shape
   reasoning, and a backend implementation.
6. A device runtime owns streams, events, synchronization, and a memory
   allocator. Asynchronous errors and allocator fragmentation surface through
   this layer rather than through the model equation.
7. A distributed tensor system attaches a logical layout to a device mesh and
   defines how operators propagate or change it.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-frameworks-autodiff-contract
//| fig-cap: "One tensor operation crosses several framework contracts. Shape and alias semantics begin at the schema; transformations, compilation, runtime scheduling, and distributed placement all need compatible rules before a device kernel can run."
digraph contract {
  bgcolor="transparent";
  rankdir=TB;
  nodesep=0.45; ranksep=0.38;
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontsize=9, fontname="Helvetica", color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  code [label="model program"];
  schema [label="operator schema\nshape · dtype · aliasing"];
  dispatch [label="dispatcher\nbackend · autograd · modes"];
  ad [label="autodiff transform\nVJP · JVP · saved tensors"];
  capture [label="capture / tracing\nguards · effects · graph IR"];
  compiler [label="compiler\nfusion · lowering · code generation"];
  runtime [label="device runtime\nstreams · allocator · kernels"];
  layout [label="distributed layout\nmesh · placement · collectives", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];

  code -> schema -> dispatch -> ad -> capture -> compiler -> runtime;
  layout -> schema [style=dashed];
  layout -> compiler [style=dashed];
  layout -> runtime [style=dashed];
}
```

A custom operator is where omissions become visible. Its registration may need
an operator schema, backend kernel, fake or meta implementation for tracing,
autograd rule, batching rule, autocast policy, and distributed partitioning
rule. A registration checker can validate that these pieces are wired together;
it cannot prove that the mathematical custom derivative is correct. That still
requires a gradient check and representative eager-versus-compiled tests.

## Distributed layout is tensor semantics

A distributed tensor represents one logical value over a device mesh, the
set of devices arranged as a multidimensional grid in which each device has a
coordinate. Its
placement may be **Shard**, meaning each mesh coordinate stores part of a tensor
dimension; **Replicate**, meaning each stores the complete value; or **Partial**,
meaning each stores a contribution awaiting reduction. Partial is not a complete
logical result.

Changing placement has communication semantics. Shard to Replicate generally
requires an all-gather. Partial to Replicate requires an all-reduce, while
Partial to Shard can use reduce-scatter. Changing the sharded dimension may
require all-to-all. The framework can insert these collectives, but it cannot
make their bytes free [@pytorch2026dtensor]. The physical topology and
sustainable link rates from @sec-accelerators-networking remain constraints on
the program.

GSPMD demonstrated how a compiler can propagate a small set of sharding
annotations through a computation graph and emit a single-program,
multiple-data execution [@xu2021gspmd]. PyTorch's distributed tensor (DTensor)
is a tensor subclass with similar global-tensor semantics: its operators
perform sharded computation and issue collectives when needed, so a distributed
program can be written as if for one device [@pytorch2026dtensor]. Fully sharded data parallel (FSDP), which shards
parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across devices, integrates parameter
sharding with the dispatcher, autograd, and allocator [@zhao2023pytorch]. Manual per-device
programs expose more control but also make collective order,
global-versus-local shape, and loss normalization the programmer's
responsibility. An inconsistent mesh or collective order can
hang every rank even when each local tensor operation is valid. The parallelism
algorithms built on these interfaces are developed in @sec-training-at-scale.

## An operating checklist

Correctness comes before a speedup claim. For a new model path, operator, or
framework backend:

- Compare eager and compiled outputs, gradients, state updates, and random
  number consumption on representative inputs.
- Run a directional finite difference and the framework's gradient check in
  double precision, away from nondifferentiable points.
- Cover shape, dtype, device, layout, noncontiguous views, broadcasting,
  zero-size tensors, aliasing, and mutation. Test `NaN` and infinity behavior
  deliberately.
- Measure cold compile and warm execution separately. Record cache keys or input
  signatures, graph-break locations, guard failures, and recompilation counts.
- Profile kernel time, host gaps, saved-tensor bytes, peak memory, allocator
  reserves, and communication volume. A faster kernel can still make the whole
  step slower.
- In distributed tests, assert global and local shapes, placement transitions,
  reduction denominators, mesh identity, collective order, checkpoint restore,
  and behavior after a rank or link failure.
- State the reproducibility target: tolerance-close, statistically equivalent,
  restart-equivalent, or bitwise on one fixed platform. Purity and fixed seeds
  help, but compiler paths, reduction order, world size, hardware, and releases
  can still change exact bits.

The serving incidents that arise from compilation caches, allocator behavior,
and backend coverage continue in @sec-serving-problem.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Lower-layer constraint

The framework cannot erase the machine underneath it. Supported dtypes, memory
layouts, tile shapes, collective bandwidth, and compiler coverage determine
which operator contracts can be implemented efficiently. Conversely, an
architecture whose central operation lacks a correct derivative, lowering, or
distributed rule may be uneconomical to evaluate even if its mathematics is
promising. @sec-compilers-kernels follows this constraint from captured graph to
device code.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

The open question is where the durable abstraction boundary should sit. One
view favors a rich eager framework whose compiler captures compatible regions;
another favors pure staged programs whose transformations are explicit; a third
pushes more semantics into portable operator and compiler interfaces. These
approaches trade debugging freedom, compilation scope, custom-kernel control,
and backend portability. None removes the need to specify derivatives, effects,
layouts, and failure behavior. A framework becomes portable only to the extent
that those contracts have working implementations on the target system.
:::
